name: Gwarpatha
actions: Cooling and soothing on the skin
Laxative (the yellow latex, not the gel)
traditionalUses: Minor burns and sunburn (gel on skin)
kitchenUse: Clear inner gel from the leaf applied to skin. Wash off the yellow latex first.

typicalUse.note: Taking aloe latex by mouth is a strong laxative and is not advised. Whole-leaf (non-decolourised) extract is classed by IARC as a possible human carcinogen; the clear gel on the skin is the safest use.

cautions.note: Aloe gel, latex or whole-leaf extract taken by mouth may be unsafe in pregnancy.
Aloe taken by mouth may be unsafe while breastfeeding.
Aloe leaf extracts taken by mouth have been linked to acute hepatitis.
Oral aloe latex can harm the kidneys with regular use.
Do not give aloe by mouth to children.
The gel is usually well tolerated, but it occasionally causes burning, itching or a rash.

interactions.effect: Oral aloe may lower blood sugar further.
Oral latex can lower potassium with water pills.
Overuse of aloe latex can increase side effects of digoxin.

evidence.summary: Clinical research suggests the gel on the skin may speed burn healing and reduce burn pain. Evidence for oral use is weak.

sources.title: The Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I
NCCIH: Aloe Vera: Usefulness and Safety
